lessonTitle: The Prescribing Process and Medicines Reconciliation

blocks.text: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted with a chest infection. Nobody reconciles his medicines, so his time-critical levodopa preparation is not prescribed for the first 36 hours. He becomes rigid and unable to swallow, aspirates, and spends a week in hospital that would not otherwise have been needed. The error was not in the choice of drug or dose; it was in the process that connects a decision to a patient receiving the right medicine at the right time.

blocks.markdown: **Safe prescribing is a process, not a single act.** At each step there are things to check, and each step can fail. The process runs from the **indication** through to **review**, and it is described in GMC guidance on prescribing and in NICE guidance on medicines optimisation. Work within your competence, involve the patient in decisions, take responsibility for what you prescribe, and keep clear records.

items: Gather information: the diagnosis and indication, the patient's history, allergies and previous adverse reactions, current medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal), renal and hepatic function, weight, pregnancy and the patient's preferences.
Decide whether a medicine is needed at all, and what the goal is; consider non-drug options and shared decision-making.
Choose the drug using guidelines, the BNF and local formulary, checking contraindications, cautions and interactions.
Choose dose, route, frequency, duration and formulation, adjusting for the patient.
Write a clear, complete, legal prescription.
Communicate: counsel the patient, and inform the team, pharmacy and GP.
Monitor and review: effect, adverse effects, adherence and continued need, with a review or stop date.

blocks.title: The patient is part of the process
blocks.text: Check what the patient understands and wants. Many errors are caught by asking the patient or carer, 'What do you take this for, and when?' Counselling about purpose, how to take the medicine, important adverse effects and what to do if concerned improves adherence and safety (see the unit on adherence).

blocks.markdown: **Medicines reconciliation** is the process of obtaining an accurate list of everything the patient is taking, comparing it with the prescribing plan and resolving discrepancies, at every transition of care. NICE guidance on medicines optimisation recommends that it be done as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of admission, by a person with the necessary skills. The aim is a **best possible medication history**, built from **at least two sources**, with the patient or carer interview complemented by a documented record. Reconciling is more than copying a list: you must verify what is actually taken, including doses, timing, formulation, adherence, over-the-counter products and recent changes.

rows: Patient or carer interview
Reveals what is really taken and adherence, including over-the-counter and herbal products
Memory and health literacy limit accuracy
GP record or Summary Care Record
Authoritative repeat prescription list
May not reflect recent hospital or specialist changes, or what is actually taken
Patient's own medicines or dispensed packs
Shows what has been supplied, strengths and labels
May be out of date or incomplete; not proof of use
Community pharmacy records, care home administration charts
Shows what has been dispensed or administered
May lag behind recent changes
Previous discharge letters, specialist clinic letters
Recent changes and rationale
May be outdated or incomplete
blocks.caption: Sources for a best possible medication history. Use at least two and resolve differences.

blocks.title: Reconciling medicines at admission
blocks.prompt: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with a fall. The GP list shows ramipril, bisoprolol, furosemide and atorvastatin. She tells you she also takes 'a blood thinner started in hospital three weeks ago' and ibuprofen for her knee, bought at the pharmacy. Her own bag contains an anticoagulant pack labelled by the hospital pharmacy. Reconcile her list.

steps.text: Identify the sources and compare them: GP list (four items), patient interview (extra anticoagulant and ibuprofen), and her own supplied pack (confirms the anticoagulant with a dispensing date). Together they provide three sources that agree on the anticoagulant, which the GP list lacks because it was started recently by the hospital.

Classify the discrepancies: the anticoagulant is an unintentional omission from the GP list (not a deliberate decision), and ibuprofen is an unrecorded over-the-counter medicine. Both are clinically important: an anticoagulant with an NSAID increases bleeding risk, and an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic increases acute kidney injury risk.

Verify the details: dose, frequency, indication, start date and last dose taken, from the supplied pack, the previous discharge letter or the pharmacy. Confirm adherence and what time each medicine is taken.

Act and document: prescribe the verified medicines (continuing the anticoagulant, with the time of the next dose), review whether ibuprofen should continue given the risks, record the reconciled list with sources used, date and your name, and communicate changes to the GP at discharge.

blocks.answer: Three sources identified a missing anticoagulant and an unrecorded NSAID. Verify, prescribe the right regular medicines, address the NSAID, and document sources and decisions.

rows: Intentional, documented
A deliberate change with a recorded reason
Medicine stopped for acute kidney injury, reason noted
Intentional, undocumented
A deliberate change but no record of why
Dose reduced without a note, which confuses the next team
Unintentional omission
A regular medicine left off the list
Inhaler or time-critical drug not prescribed
Unintentional commission or dose error
A drug added, or wrong dose, frequency or formulation
Duplicate brand and generic, wrong strength
blocks.caption: Types of discrepancy found at reconciliation.

blocks.markdown: **At discharge**, reconcile the discharge list against the pre-admission list and the inpatient chart. Every medicine should be either continued, changed (with the reason), stopped (with the reason) or started (with indication and duration). The discharge communication to the GP and community pharmacy must state changes made and why, doses and frequencies, the duration of short courses, monitoring required (for example blood tests after a change to a renally active drug) and who is responsible for it. Discharge supply should be enough for the patient until the GP can supply. A single clear list for the patient avoids confusion, and the patient should be counselled on any changes.

**A legal, complete and unambiguous prescription.** Prescriptions in the UK must meet the requirements of the Human Medicines Regulations and local policy; the BNF and your organisation's prescribing policy set out the current details. For a hospital inpatient chart, the essential elements are: patient identifiers (full name and a unique number or date of birth), allergy status, weight where relevant, the drug written by its **approved (generic) name** (brand names only when they matter, such as modified-release preparations or some narrow-therapeutic-index drugs), the **dose** (with units), **route**, **frequency** (and time, for time-critical drugs), **indication** where required, start date and **duration or review date**, and signature and name (or electronic equivalent). For as-required drugs, include the indication, the minimum interval and the maximum dose in 24 hours. Controlled drugs have additional legal requirements, including the total quantity in words and figures on a controlled drug prescription. Write legibly, in indelible ink or electronically, and avoid ambiguity.

rows: Units
Write micrograms, nanograms, units and millilitres in full
Abbreviating micrograms, or writing 'U' for units, can be misread, with tenfold errors
Decimals
Use a leading zero (0.5 mg) and no trailing zero (5 mg)
'.5 mg' may be read as 5 mg; '5.0 mg' may be read as 50 mg
Frequency
Write 'once daily', 'twice daily' or give times
'OD' and similar abbreviations may be misread
Drug names
Use approved names; check look-alike and sound-alike pairs
Brand or abbreviated names invite confusion
Doses
State dose in mg (not number of tablets) or both
Tablets of different strengths cause errors
As-required medicines
State indication, interval and maximum in 24 hours
'PRN' alone gives no limits
blocks.caption: Writing conventions that reduce misreading. Follow local policy.

blocks.latex: \text{Total quantity} = \frac{\text{dose per administration}}{\text{tablet strength}} \times \text{administrations per day} \times \text{days}
blocks.caption: Convert units first (1 mg = 1000 micrograms) so dose and strength share units.

blocks.title: Rewriting an unsafe chart entry
blocks.prompt: A chart entry reads: 'Frusemide 40.0mg od po, Morphine liquid 5mg prn'. Identify the problems and rewrite it as a safe, complete prescription (teaching example; check the BNF for any real dose).

steps.text: Drug names and abbreviations: 'frusemide' is an outdated spelling, so use the approved name furosemide; 'od' is an unsafe abbreviation, so write 'once daily'; 'po' should be 'oral'.
Dose formatting: '40.0mg' has a trailing zero that could be read as 400, so write '40 mg', and leave a space between the number and the unit.

Incomplete as-required entry: 'prn' gives no indication, route, minimum interval, or maximum in 24 hours. Morphine is a controlled drug, so specify the preparation, concentration, route, dose in mg, indication, the minimum interval and a maximum daily dose, and prescribe a laxative alongside if regular.

Add the missing legal and safety elements: patient identifiers, allergy status, start date, signature and printed name, and a review date. Rewritten example: 'Furosemide 40 mg oral once daily, 08:00. Indication: heart failure. Review: 3 days.'

blocks.answer: Use approved names, write once daily and oral in full, remove the trailing zero, complete the as-required details and add identifiers, allergy status, date and signature.

blocks.title: Do not copy forward errors
blocks.text: Rewriting a chart or discharge list by copying an earlier list perpetuates mistakes, including doses that were changed and medicines that were stopped. Reconcile against current sources, check each item's indication, and take responsibility for what you sign.

points: Safe prescribing runs from information gathering and indication through choice of drug and dose, a clear prescription, communication, and monitoring and review.
Medicines reconciliation aims for a best possible medication history from at least two sources, ideally within 24 hours of admission, and the discrepancies are classified and resolved.
At discharge reconcile the list and communicate every change and its reason, with duration and monitoring, to the patient, GP and pharmacy.
A safe prescription has patient identifiers, allergy status, approved drug name, dose with units, route, frequency, indication where required, duration or review date and signature.
Write units in full, use a leading zero and no trailing zero, avoid unsafe abbreviations, and give limits for as-required drugs.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the main steps of safe prescribing?
questions.explanation: Each step of the process can fail, so structured thinking prevents most errors. Review closes the loop by checking benefit, harm and continued need.

options.text: Choose the drug, write the prescription, then find out the diagnosis
Gather information and confirm the indication, choose treatment, write the prescription, communicate, then monitor and review
Write the prescription, then check allergies, then review in a year
Copy the previous prescription and review only if the patient complains

questions.correctOptionText: Gather information and confirm the indication, choose treatment, write the prescription, communicate, then monitor and review

distractorRationale.a: The diagnosis and indication must come first.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: information gathering and indication lead to a choice of treatment, a clear prescription, communication and review.
distractorRationale.c: Allergies should be checked before prescribing, and review needs a defined date.
distractorRationale.d: Copying forward perpetuates errors and omits review.

questions.stem: A patient has taken a proton pump inhibitor for two years 'for stomach protection', started during a course of oral steroids that finished long ago. Which step of safe prescribing has most clearly failed?
questions.explanation: Recording an indication and a review or stop date allows later clinicians to challenge continued treatment. Without them, medicines continue by default.

options.text: Choosing the drug
Writing the prescription legibly
Monitoring and review with a stop or review date
Counselling about the first dose

questions.correctOptionText: Monitoring and review with a stop or review date

distractorRationale.a: The original choice may have been appropriate.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: no review or stop date led to continuation beyond the original indication.
distractorRationale.d: Counselling at the start does not explain continuation.

questions.stem: What does a best possible medication history require?
questions.explanation: A single source seldom gives a complete and accurate list. Cross-checking sources and verifying details such as dose and last dose taken is the essence of reconciliation.

options.text: One source only, whichever is quickest
At least two sources, including an interview with the patient or carer where possible, and verification of what is actually taken
A copy of the GP list without discussion
Only the medicines on the admission drug chart

questions.correctOptionText: At least two sources, including an interview with the patient or carer where possible, and verification of what is actually taken

distractorRationale.a: One source can be incomplete or out of date.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: multiple sources, including the patient or carer, verify what is really taken.
distractorRationale.c: A GP list may not reflect recent changes or over-the-counter use.
distractorRationale.d: The admission chart is what you are checking, not the source of truth.

questions.stem: What must the medication information given at discharge include?
questions.explanation: Poor communication at discharge is a major cause of harm after discharge. Clear reasons for changes help the GP and community pharmacy to continue or review treatment safely.

options.text: Only the medicines that are new
Every medicine with whether it is continued, changed, stopped or started, the reasons for changes, and any monitoring required
Only the medicines the patient requests
The ward drug chart without explanation

questions.correctOptionText: Every medicine with whether it is continued, changed, stopped or started, the reasons for changes, and any monitoring required

distractorRationale.a: Continuing and stopped medicines are equally important to communicate.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the GP and pharmacy need the full reconciled picture and the reasons.
distractorRationale.c: Patient preference matters but is not the basis of the list.
distractorRationale.d: A chart without explanation does not convey what changed and why.

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to write a dose of half a milligram on a prescription?
questions.explanation: Safe writing conventions reduce misreading: use a leading zero before a decimal point, avoid trailing zeros and write units in full. Tenfold errors are among the most harmful prescribing errors.

options.text: .5 mg
1/2 mg
0.5 mg

distractorRationale.a: A missing leading zero can be read as 5 mg.
distractorRationale.b: A trailing zero can be misread as a larger number.
distractorRationale.c: Fractions are ambiguous and easily misread.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: a leading zero and no trailing zero reduce the risk of tenfold errors.

questions.stem: True or false: medicines reconciliation need only be performed at admission.
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is needed at every transition of care, including transfers between wards and discharge. Changes during admission have to be communicated to the next provider, or errors enter the community.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: A hypothetical drug is prescribed at 1.5 mg twice daily for 14 days, and is supplied as 500 microgram tablets. How many tablets should be supplied in total?
questions.explanation: Convert 1.5 mg to 1500 micrograms, which is 3 tablets of 500 micrograms per dose. With twice-daily dosing that is 6 tablets per day, and over 14 days the total is 84 tablets.

questions.stem: An audit of 120 admitted patients found that 18 had at least one unintentional discrepancy in their medicines on admission. What percentage of audited patients had an unintentional discrepancy?
questions.explanation: The proportion is 18 divided by 120, which equals 0.15. This is 15%, a figure that can be tracked over time to judge whether reconciliation processes are improving.

questions.stem: List the essential elements of a safe, complete and legal inpatient prescription, and describe the writing conventions that reduce misreading.
questions.explanation: A strong answer covers identification, the drug details, timing and limits, and signature, and links writing conventions to specific misreading errors. It should mention the extra requirements for controlled drugs.
markingGuide: Patient identifiers (full name and unique number or date of birth), allergy status, weight where relevant
Approved (generic) drug name; brand only where it matters
Dose with units, route, frequency or time, indication where required
Start date, duration or review date for short courses
For as-required drugs: indication, minimum interval and maximum dose in 24 hours
Legible, indelible or electronic, signed with printed name or electronic equivalent; additional controlled drug requirements
Conventions: units in full (micrograms), leading zero and no trailing zero, avoid unsafe abbreviations and look-alike names

questions.stem: A 70-year-old is being discharged after an admission with heart failure. Over the stay, furosemide was increased, spironolactone was started and ramipril was paused because of acute kidney injury. Describe how you would reconcile and communicate his medicines at discharge.
questions.explanation: The key point is that discharge communication must explain what changed and why, and must make monitoring and responsibility explicit. Paused or stopped drugs are as important to communicate as new ones.
markingGuide: Reconcile the discharge list against the pre-admission list and the inpatient chart, using current sources and verifying with the patient
Classify each medicine as continued, changed, stopped or started, with the reason (for example ramipril paused for acute kidney injury and when to review restarting it)
Check doses, indications and interactions, for example the combination of spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor if restarted (hyperkalaemia and renal function)
Specify monitoring: urea and electrolytes within a stated time after discharge, who will do it and who acts on the results
Provide a clear written list to the patient with counselling, and send a clear summary to the GP and community pharmacy
Arrange adequate supply, record the sources used, and document responsibilities
